overview:
Kayotsarga (Sanskrit: "kāyotsarga", Jain Prakrit: "kāussagga") is a central contemplative and ascetic posture in Jain practice, literally meaning "abandonment" or "dismissal of the body". Etymologically, it is formed from "kāya" (body) and "utsarga" (letting go, renunciation), and thus denotes a deliberate loosening of identification with the physical body and its comforts. In classical descriptions, the practitioner stands or sits absolutely still, withdrawing attention from bodily sensations and movements, and directing awareness toward the true nature of the soul (jīva) as distinct from the body.

In the ritual and doctrinal framework of Jainism, kayotsarga is counted among the six essential duties (āvaśyaka) of an ascetic and is also integrated into lay practices such as sāmāyika (periods of equanimity and meditation) and pratikramaṇa (confession and repentance). During sāmāyika, after bowing to the Pañca-Parameṣṭhi and reciting the Namokāra mantra, the practitioner engages in a sequence of inner acts—pratikramaṇa, pratyākhyāna, sāmāyika-karma, stuti, vandanā—and finally kayotsarga, understood as withdrawal of attention from the body and absorption in contemplation of the spiritual self. In this sense, kayotsarga is not merely a physical pose but a structured meditative act of renunciation of attachment (parigraha) and cultivation of equanimity (samatā).

Historically, kayotsarga is closely associated with the iconography and biographies of the Tīrthaṅkaras and exemplary ascetics. Jain images often depict Tīrthaṅkaras either seated in meditation or standing in kayotsarga, with the body upright, arms hanging loosely, and feet slightly apart, symbolizing unwavering detachment. Traditional narratives state that many Tīrthaṅkaras attained liberation (mokṣa) while in the standing kayotsarga posture, and the story of Bahubali is frequently cited: he is said to have stood in kayotsarga for a year, remaining motionless despite vines growing around his legs, signifying complete non-attachment to bodily conditions.

Ritual manuals and commentarial literature elaborate kayotsarga as a form of "ritualized meditation". In texts such as the Āvaśyaka-sūtra and its commentaries, kayotsarga appears in formulaic prescriptions as part of daily obligatory rites for both monks and laity, especially in the context of pratikramaṇa. The practice is linked to several aims: cessation of harmful activity (particularly the inadvertent injury to living beings caused by movement), purification of the soul from sinful karmas, performance of penance (prāyaścitta), special purification of mental states (viśodhikaraṇa), removal of inner "thorns" such as deceit and false belief (viśallikaraṇa), and reverential worship of the Arhats and scriptures. In some lay-progress schemes (pratimā systems), kayotsarga also names a stage in which the practitioner undertakes more intensive restraint, including spending nights in kayotsarga posture or abstaining from food after sunset.

From a doctrinal perspective, kayotsarga is closely tied to Jain teachings on karma and the distinction between body and soul. By remaining motionless and mentally detached, the practitioner minimizes new karmic influx (āsrava) associated with bodily activity and begins to weaken existing karmic bonds (bandha). The inner attitude is one of seeing the body as a temporary aggregate of matter (pudgala) and recognizing the soul as inherently endowed with knowledge and perception. Commentarial and modern expositions emphasize that the essence of kayotsarga lies in this experiential insight: the practitioner "stands" or "sits" in awareness of being more than the body, using stillness as a support for contemplation of the self's purity and for repentance of transgressions against right knowledge, right perception, right conduct, and ascetic discipline.

In contemporary Jain practice, kayotsarga continues to be performed in both sectarian and non-sectarian contexts. It appears in traditional pratikramaṇa liturgies, in lay sāmāyika observances, and in modern meditation systems such as prekṣā-dhyāna, where it may be presented as a technique of relaxation and concentration rooted in ancient ascetic methods. While external forms—standing, sitting, duration—vary according to lineage and capacity, the core meaning remains consistent: kayotsarga is the disciplined, reverent act of letting go of bodily attachment in order to remember and realize the soul's true nature, within the ethical framework of non-violence and self-restraint.

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain canonical redactors; exact authorship and date are contested
primary_sources.original_text: इच्छामि ठाणे काउस्सग्गं तस्स उत्तरिकरणेण पयच्चित्तकरणेण विसोधिकरणेण विसल्लिकरणेण पापाणं कम्माणं निग्घातणाहाए ठाणे काउस्सग्गं। तावकारियं ठाणेण मोणेण झाणेण अप्पाणं वोसिरामि।
primary_sources.transliteration: icchāmi ṭhāṇe kāussaggaṃ tassa uttarikaraṇeṇa payacchittakaraṇeṇa visodhikaraṇeṇa visallikaraṇeṇa pāpāṇaṃ kammāṇaṃ nigghāṭaṇāhāe ṭhāṇe kāussaggaṃ. tāvakāriyaṃ ṭhāṇeṇa moṇeṇa jhāṇeṇa appāṇaṃ vosirāmi.
primary_sources.translation: “I desire to stand in kayotsarga for the sake of further excellence, for the performance of penance, for purification, for the removal of thorns, and for the destruction of sinful karmas; I stand in kayotsarga. In this way, by standing, by silence, by meditation, I let my self become detached.”
primary_sources.notes: This formula appears in the kayotsarga section of the Āvaśyaka-sūtra and its commentaries, where kayotsarga is prescribed as part of the daily obligatory rites (āvaśyaka) for ascetics and lay practitioners. The passage explicitly links kayotsarga with prāyaścitta (penance), viśodhikaraṇa (purification), viśallikaraṇa (removal of inner ‘thorns’), and the destruction of sinful karmas, emphasizing both the physical posture (standing) and the inner acts of silence and meditation.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain canonical redactors
primary_sources.translation: “One who has abandoned the body is called an ascetic.”
primary_sources.notes: This line, cited in discussions of kayotsarga, uses the term "vosaṭṭhakāe" (Prakrit for "one who has given up the body" or attachment to the body). Commentators connect this expression with the ideal embodied in kayotsarga: the true ascetic is defined by the abandonment of bodily attachment, which kayotsarga ritualizes through motionless posture and focused contemplation.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain canonical redactors
primary_sources.translation: “(He is) an ascetic who has given up the body.”
primary_sources.notes: Although the term "kayotsarga" itself does not appear in the Ācārāṅga-sūtra, the expression "kayaṃ vosajjamaṅgāre" is cited in scholarship as an early conceptual precursor. It describes the ascetic who has ‘given up’ the body, resonating with the later technical sense of kayotsarga as the practice of dismissing bodily attachment. This shows that the idea of bodily abandonment as a mark of asceticism predates the fully developed ritual terminology.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (sectarian attributions vary)
primary_sources.notes: While wording varies slightly across editions and commentaries, Tattvārtha-sūtra defines kayotsarga in relation to the stopping of bodily, verbal, and mental activity (yoga). In the broader karmic theory of the text, reduction of yoga is essential for preventing new karmic influx (āsrava). Kayotsarga, as a deliberate cessation of bodily movement combined with inner detachment, is thus framed as a technical means of restraining activity and supporting liberation.

primary_sources.title: Pratikramaṇa liturgy (Sāmāyika and Kayotsarga section)
primary_sources.author: Canonical and post-canonical liturgical redactors; specific authorship varies by sect
primary_sources.original_text: करेमि भन्ते सव्वदुज्जोणं सव्वदुज्जोणस्स कारणं सव्वदुज्जोणस्स अनुमोदणं सव्वदुज्जोणस्स निम्माणं मनसा वचसा कायेण न करिस्सामि न कारेप्पेमि न अनुमोदिस्सामि। इच्च्छामि ठाणे काउस्सग्गं।
primary_sources.transliteration: karemi bhante savvadujjoṇaṃ savvadujjoṇassa kāraṇaṃ savvadujjoṇassa anumodaṇaṃ savvadujjoṇassa nimmāṇaṃ manasā vacasā kāyeṇa na karissāmi na kāreppemi na anumodissāmi. icchāmi ṭhāṇe kāussaggaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: “Revered one, I confess all sinful activities, the causes of sinful activities, the approval of sinful activities, and the production of sinful activities; by mind, speech, and body I will not do them, will not cause them to be done, and will not approve them. I desire to stand in kayotsarga.”
primary_sources.notes: This liturgical passage, found in pratikramaṇa manuals, links the vow of kayotsarga to a prior confession and renunciation of sinful activity (savadya-yoga). The practitioner first resolves to avoid harmful actions in mind, speech, and body, and then enters kayotsarga. The sequence underscores that kayotsarga is not an isolated physical exercise but part of a moral and contemplative process of repentance and purification.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is only a physical standing posture and can be reduced to simply ‘standing still’ like a statue.
misconceptions.reality: Classical sources and liturgies describe kayotsarga as a combined physical and mental discipline: the practitioner withdraws attention from the body, undertakes silence and meditation, repents past transgressions, and contemplates the soul’s true nature. The posture supports inner detachment, but the essence of kayotsarga lies in renunciation of bodily attachment and karmic purification, not in mere immobility.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is an extreme or dangerous austerity comparable to prolonged fasting or self-harm, and is only for advanced ascetics.
misconceptions.reality: While kayotsarga is indeed a serious ascetic and meditative practice, it is also integrated into lay observances such as sāmāyika and pratikramaṇa in moderated forms. The focus is on ethical restraint, repentance, and contemplative detachment, not on harming the body. Responsible practice is adapted to one’s capacity and guided by qualified teachers; it should never be undertaken in ways that endanger health or bypass medical and pastoral care.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is sect-specific and belongs only to one Jain tradition, so other sects do not recognize or use it.
misconceptions.reality: The concept and practice of kayotsarga appear across Jain traditions, with both Digambara and Śvetāmbara sources discussing it in canonical texts, commentaries, and ritual manuals. Iconography of Tīrthaṅkaras in kayotsarga posture, narratives of liberation in standing meditation, and inclusion of kayotsarga in pratikramaṇa and āvaśyaka duties are shared features, even though details of posture, duration, and liturgical wording vary by lineage.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is only about stopping new karma and has no role in repentance or inner transformation.
misconceptions.reality: Primary formulas explicitly connect kayotsarga with prāyaścitta (penance), viśodhikaraṇa (purification), and viśallikaraṇa (removal of inner ‘thorns’ such as deceit and false belief). It is performed after confession of faults and with the intention to purify offenses against knowledge, perception, conduct, and asceticism. Thus, kayotsarga is both a means of reducing new karmic influx and a ritualized process of inner moral and spiritual transformation.
